Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Three years ago, at exactly seven o'clock on a Tuesday, Rangi's routine fractured. He was walking back to his truck along a quiet residential street when a man stepped from a side alley. There was no warning, just the sudden compression of space before hands grabbed his shoulders and threw him against a brick wall. A heavy metal door at the end of the passage swung wide, then slammed shut with a force that cracked against the bricks. Rangi's mind fixed on three frozen frames: his boots slipping on damp pavement, the man's weight pressing down, and a flash of streetlight catching a silver buckle. When he tries to piece the night together, he feels a heavy, hollow gap where the rest of the hours should be. The pictures stay exactly where they landed, refusing to flow into anything resembling a continuous story. Over the following weeks, Rangi's body began bracing for that same hour. By six-thirty, a familiar detachment settled over him like cold water. He found himself drifting outside his own thoughts, watching his own hands strip wire as if they belonged to someone else. At work, the rhythm of his days fractured. Job sites felt unmanageable when he couldn't walk through a door he hadn't inspected, his mind cataloguing every exit. In a new subdivision, he turned back before crossing the street, certain he could never properly assess the danger if he stepped inside. When he finally did enter an unfamiliar house to trace a fault in the wiring, he would stand in the hallway, eyes darting toward the main panel, listening for the metallic clang of a breaker or the heavy thud of a door closing elsewhere. His foreman noticed the pattern. Rangi stopped volunteering for after-hours callouts because the evening shift bled into that seven o'clock mark. At home, the silence grew heavy. When the snapshots surfaced, a sharp guilt would strike him. He had come to believe the event happened because of the sort of person he was, and what frightened him most was the certainty that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. A fear of an empty future settled in his chest alongside the hopelessness. The memories surfaced without warning. Around the same time, Rangi began spending his evenings on the couch, phone glowing in his palm. He lost hours to games and scrolling, deliberately steering clear of any television programmes or articles that might echo the assault. The whiskey bottle and the pill bottle lived on the kitchen counter. When the days stretched too long, he drank and took medication, the numbness sitting beside the guilt rather than pushing it away. Unfamiliar spaces became his rule. If a new job required him to navigate a floor plan he hadn't walked before, he stood at the threshold, scanning, calculating, and often walking out. Startle responses took over his daily rhythm. A colleague patting his back on the job site sent him jerking forward, heart hammering. A sudden shift of a customer's hand near him triggered the same rigid alarm. His partner, Lina, tried to understand, but the distance grew. The alcohol and the screen time built walls he couldn't explain, and the guilt of his own withdrawal only deepened the nights he couldn't sleep. It was Lina who finally asked him to see a counselor, noting how he flinched when the front door clicked shut at seven. Rangi agreed, not because he expected the dread to lift, but because the weight of carrying the pieces alone had become unbearable. He sat in the therapist's office hoping for a way to stop feeling like the past was a room he could never leave, terrified that if he stopped running, the rest of the story would finally catch up to him.
